sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll build a mental model for five concepts that will make you a better AI user for the rest of your life: **tokens**, **context windows**, **prediction**, **temperature**, and **training vs. runtime**. Understanding these isn't optional — they explain almost every quirk, limitation, and capability of every AI tool you'll ever use.

No math. No code. Just accurate mental models.

## The Core Idea: Next-Token Prediction

At the most fundamental level, a language model does one thing: **predict the most likely next token** given everything that came before it.

A **token** is roughly a word or word-fragment. The sentence *"The cat sat on the mat"* is about 7 tokens. Claude processes everything — your question, the conversation history, its instructions — as a sequence of tokens.

When you send Claude a message, it doesn't "think" the way humans do. It repeatedly runs one calculation: *given all the tokens so far, what token should come next?* It does this thousands of times per second to generate a response.

This sounds too simple to produce intelligent output. But trained on enough data, next-token prediction turns out to be a surprisingly deep skill. To predict what comes next in text about physics, medicine, code, or poetry, you have to implicitly learn a lot about physics, medicine, code, and poetry.

**The critical implication:** Claude doesn't "know" things the way you know your own name. It generates responses that are statistically likely given the training data. Usually that's right. Sometimes it's confidently wrong — which is what hallucination is.

**The cooking analogy:** A language model is like a chef who has eaten at a million restaurants. They don't have a rulebook for every cuisine — they've absorbed so many patterns that they can produce authentic-tasting food in any style. They're not *copying* recipes; they've internalised the underlying logic — and they can produce a dish they've never made before by combining patterns they have seen.

## Tokens — The Currency of AI

Tokens are how AI models measure and price everything. Understanding tokens makes you a better AI user and helps you understand costs if you ever build with the API.

**Token sizes:**
- 1 token ≈ 4 characters in English
- 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word
- 100 tokens ≈ 75 words
- 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words ≈ 1.5 pages

**What gets tokenised:**
- Your question: tokens
- Previous messages in the conversation: tokens
- The system prompt (Claude's instructions): tokens
- Claude's response: tokens

All of these together must fit within the context window (see below).

**Why token boundaries matter:**
Some words are multiple tokens. "Unbelievable" might be split: "Un" + "believ" + "able". Numbers and code are often tokenised differently from prose. This is why AI sometimes makes odd errors mid-word — the model's prediction can go wrong at a token boundary.

**Tokens and cost:**
When you use the API (building your own tools), you pay per million tokens. A 1,000-token prompt costs 4× as much to send repeatedly as a 250-token prompt. This is why professional AI users think carefully about prompt length — not just for quality, but for cost.

## The Context Window — Working Memory

Every LLM has a **context window** — the maximum amount of text it can "see" and reason about at once. Think of it as the model's working memory.

Everything inside the context window, the model knows. Everything outside it, the model has no access to.

This is why:
- Claude doesn't remember your conversation from yesterday (that conversation is gone — outside the window)
- Very long documents can hit limits (the document might not fit in the window)
- Starting a new chat "resets" Claude (empty context = no memory of previous chats)

**Context windows in 2026:**
- Claude: ~200,000 tokens (roughly a 150,000-word novel — or about 500 pages)
- GPT-4o: ~128,000 tokens
- Gemini 2.5 Pro: ~1,000,000 tokens (an entire year of dense reading)

**What fills the context window:**
At any point in a conversation, the context contains: the system prompt + all previous messages + the current message. Long conversations eat context, which is why very long chats sometimes produce less sharp responses — the model's working memory is filling up.

**Practical implication:** If you want Claude to remember something across sessions, you have to give it that information yourself. Paste it in, upload a file, or use Claude's Projects feature to persist context.

**The information order effect:** Claude (and all LLMs) tends to pay more attention to information at the beginning and end of the context window. If you have a long document and a specific question, put your question *first*, before the document — not after it. This is counterintuitive (humans usually read context then ask questions) but produces better AI results.

## Temperature — Controlling Creativity vs. Consistency

When an AI model predicts the next token, it generates a probability distribution over all possible tokens. Temperature is a parameter that controls how the model samples from that distribution.

**Low temperature (close to 0):**
- The model almost always picks the most probable next token
- Output is consistent, predictable, and focused
- Use for: factual questions, code generation, formal writing, tasks where you want the same answer each time

**High temperature (close to 1 or above):**
- The model samples more broadly, occasionally picking lower-probability tokens
- Output is more varied, creative, and surprising — but less reliable
- Use for: brainstorming, creative writing, generating options

In Claude.ai (the consumer interface), you don't control temperature directly — Anthropic sets it for you at a sensible default. But if you use the Claude API, you can set it explicitly. Understanding temperature helps explain why:
- The same question can get slightly different answers in different conversations (sampling variation)
- AI sometimes produces unexpected word choices (temperature lets lower-probability tokens occasionally "win")
- Some AI outputs are remarkably consistent while others vary noticeably

**The determinism myth:** Many people assume AI is deterministic — same input, same output. It's usually not. Temperature-based sampling means the same prompt generates slightly different responses. Some developers set temperature to 0 for fully deterministic output (useful for automated testing), but this makes the output more robotic.

## Training vs. Runtime — Two Completely Different Things

There are two distinct phases of an AI model's life:

**Training** — The model learns by processing billions of documents and adjusting its internal parameters to get better at next-token prediction. This happens once (or periodically at massive cost). You don't control this.

**Runtime (inference)** — When you send a message, the trained model uses its learned parameters to generate a response. This is what happens every time you use Claude. It's much cheaper and faster than training.

**Why this distinction matters:**
- The model's *knowledge* comes from training (has a cutoff date)
- The model's *behaviour* in a conversation depends on what's in the context window at runtime
- You can dramatically change what the model does at runtime using the context window — without changing the model itself
- This is what "prompting" is: runtime-level instruction that shapes behaviour without changing training

**What RLHF is (and why Claude isn't just a raw language model):**
Raw language models are capable but wild — they'll generate anything, helpful or not. Anthropic trains Claude with **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)**: human raters evaluate responses and score them for helpfulness, accuracy, and safety. The model is then trained to prefer responses humans rated highly.

This is why Claude is *helpful* (not just capable), declines harmful requests, and hedges appropriately when uncertain. The core model is the same; RLHF shaped how it uses that core capability.

## System Prompts — The Invisible Instructions

Every conversation with Claude has three layers:
1. **System prompt** — Instructions set by whoever deployed Claude (Anthropic, an app, a company) before you ever send a message. Invisible to you.
2. **Your messages** — What you type.
3. **Claude's responses** — What Claude generates.

The system prompt is powerful: it can tell Claude to adopt a persona, restrict what topics it will discuss, specify a response format, provide background context, or change how it behaves. When you use Claude.ai directly, Anthropic sets the system prompt. When a company integrates Claude into their product, *they* set the system prompt — which is why the same underlying model behaves differently in different apps.

**Why this matters for you as a user:**
- If Claude behaves oddly in a particular app, it might be following a system prompt you can't see
- When you build with the Claude API (later in this course), you'll write your own system prompts
- Understanding that a system prompt exists helps explain why the same question gets different answers in different Claude products

**You can simulate a system prompt** in Claude.ai by putting instructions at the start of your very first message in a conversation. This isn't as reliable as an actual system prompt, but it works well enough for most use cases.

sections.title: The Context Window Experiment + Temperature Discovery
sections.content:
Two experiments in one — both make concepts visceral and unforgettable.

**Experiment 1 — The Context Window (10 minutes)**

1. Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and paste a long Wikipedia article (3,000+ words — try the article on "World War II" or "Climate change").
2. Ask Claude to summarise it in three bullet points. It will do it perfectly — the full article is in its context window.
3. Ask a specific question about a detail mentioned in the article (a date, a name, a specific event). It answers correctly.
4. Start a **brand new conversation** (click "New Chat"). Ask Claude the same specific question without pasting anything.
5. Notice that Claude either doesn't know the answer or gives a generic response. The article was never in *this* conversation's context window.

**Write two sentences:**
1. What the context window is (in your own words)
2. One practical implication for how you'll use AI going forward

**Experiment 2 — Temperature in Action (5 minutes)**

In the same conversation as Experiment 1, send this prompt three times (just hit the send button three times with the same text):
```
Give me a single creative metaphor for the concept of a 'context window'.
```

Are all three responses the same? Different? How different?

**Write one sentence:** What does the variation between responses tell you about how AI generation works?

**Experiment 3 — System Prompt Simulation (5 minutes)**

Start a new chat. As your *very first message* (before asking anything else), write:
```
For this conversation: You are a blunt, direct expert who gives opinions not options. You never hedge. When I ask a question, give me your clearest recommendation, not a list of considerations.
```

Then ask a question that normally produces a hedge-filled response: *"Should I learn Python or JavaScript first?"*

Compare the response to what you normally get without the instruction. Did the system-prompt-style instruction change the output?

sections.question: You paste a 5,000-word document into Claude and have a long conversation about it over 30 turns. Near the end of the conversation, you notice Claude's responses about the document seem less precise and sometimes miss details it got right earlier. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Claude gets tired and less accurate over long conversations
The conversation history has grown long enough to push some of the original document content toward the edges of the context window, where models pay less attention
The document is corrupted and Claude can no longer read it correctly
You need to upgrade to Claude Pro for long conversations
sections.explanation: As a conversation grows, all the previous messages accumulate and fill the context window. The original document is still there, but it may now be buried under dozens of conversation turns. LLMs tend to attend more strongly to recent context and less to earlier context that's now far from the active position in the window. The fix: start a new conversation with the document fresh, or summarise the conversation so far and include that summary with the document in a new chat.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 1-2.** You now understand tokens, context windows, next-token prediction, temperature, the training/runtime distinction, RLHF, and system prompts. These five concepts explain almost every behaviour you'll observe in AI tools — both impressive capabilities and frustrating limitations.
